purpose: Bounded Federal Reserve 2025 SHED route from labor-market mobility and worker-reported generative-AI use through task control and perceived benefit, preserving employer policy, realized productivity, household, and exit gaps.

events.geography: United States; Federal Reserve 2025 Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking
events.date_precision: 2025 survey release; measures cover prior-month AI use and current work conditions, exact episode dates not retained
events.denominator: Published worker and employee bases; AI use, education, task-control, work-location, and schedule measures have distinct denominators
events.method: Federal Reserve published descriptive SHED estimates for employment movement, worker-reported generative-AI use, perceived benefit, education, task control, location, and schedule variation
events.missingness: Tool, task, intensity, employer policy, implementation date, pay, hours, training, monitoring, bargaining, household effect, and later outcome are not retained
events.exposure: 25% of workers reported using generative AI in the prior month; use was 10% among workers with high-school education or less versus 43% among workers with graduate degrees, and 30% among employees with high task control versus 20% with lower task control
events.alternatives_before_action: Alternative tools, training, employer permission, non-AI work routes, worker voice, and job-switching options are not observed for the same respondent
events.immediate_burden_or_benefit: Among workers, 44% agreed generative AI saves time in their job; among AI users, 52% said it improved quality. These are perceived benefits, not measured productivity or pay
events.choice_or_response: The survey also reports labor-market friction and work-organization conditions: 7% of adults reported a layoff in 2025, 8% voluntarily left a job, and 39% of workers worked from home during the prior week
events.person_or_actor_with_control: Workers report task control and AI use, but employer permission, deployment rules, monitoring, training, and control over resulting data or evaluation are not identified
events.remedy_or_institutional_response: No employer correction, bargaining response, public rule, complaint, or remedy is observed
events.immediate_outcome: The SHED layer establishes unequal worker access/control and perceived AI benefit alongside labor mobility and work-organization conditions
events.protected_outcome: AI time or quality gains could protect worker capacity, but no realized earnings, hours, health, or household protection is measured
events.sacrificed_outcome: Unequal access or lower task control could limit gains or increase monitoring/dependence, but no realized sacrifice is measured
events.cost_risk_transfer: The source does not identify whether technology cost, productivity gain, training burden, or employment risk transfers among firms and workers
events.later_outcome: No same-worker later productivity, pay, job quality, household security, trust, political response, switching, or exit is observed
events.meaning_and_attribution: Workers' perceived benefit and control measures describe experience but do not identify employer intent, fairness, attribution, or bargaining meaning
events.public_or_collective_response: No organizing, bargaining, complaint, policy response, or collective action endpoint is linked
events.counterexample: AI use can be higher where workers have more control and education, but that may reflect task fit, job composition, employer permission, or resources rather than control causing adoption
events.source_and_uncertainty: Federal Reserve 2025 SHED published estimates; cross-sectional subgroup comparisons do not establish causality, worker-level transition, or realized AI effects

arrows.evidence: Published subgroup shares show 43% use among workers with graduate degrees versus 10% with high school or less, and 30% use among employees with high task control versus 20% with lower task control
arrows.counterexample: Education and task-control groups are not a worker panel; occupation, industry, employer permission, and task fit may explain the difference
arrows.remaining_gap: Same-worker timing, task exposure, employer policy, training, and causal access mechanism

arrows.evidence: Among workers, 44% agreed AI saves time; among AI users, 52% agreed it improved work quality
arrows.counterexample: Perceived benefit may reflect self-selection, task fit, or expectations and is not measured output, pay, or time release
arrows.remaining_gap: Tool/task intensity, objective productivity, hours, pay, quality verification, and distribution of gains

arrows.to: worker autonomy, bargaining, and job mobility
arrows.evidence: The survey places AI use and task-control subgroups beside job movement and work-organization measures, but does not link them within a worker-level panel
arrows.counterexample: Higher task control may accompany occupations with different labor demand, education, and employer policies rather than produce AI use or mobility
arrows.remaining_gap: Matched worker episodes with task change, employer rule, training, monitoring, pay/hours, retention, switching, and exit

arrows.to: household security, health, trust, or political action
arrows.evidence: The published SHED layer does not link worker AI use/control to later household, health, trust, or political outcomes
arrows.counterexample: AI use can save time without improving financial room, or reduce task burden while increasing monitoring or insecurity
arrows.remaining_gap: Same-worker and household follow-up with material outcome, institutional response, trust, action, and exit

arrows.from: unequal worker AI access and control
arrows.to: sector capability, concentration, or geopolitical leverage
arrows.evidence: The survey contains no firm, supplier, infrastructure, public-capacity, or cross-border capability link
arrows.counterexample: Worker-level access differences can reflect local capability gaps, but the survey cannot assign sector or state consequences
arrows.remaining_gap: Worker-firm-sector linkage to infrastructure, supplier dependence, public capacity, and international response

boundary: This ledger formalizes worker-reported AI access, control, perceived benefit, and labor-mobility context. It does not establish causal AI effects, realized productivity, bargaining power, household welfare, political response, or geopolitical leverage.
storage_boundary: Only published Federal Reserve aggregate estimates and source metadata are retained; no respondent microdata are stored.
